strengths: The combination of AGOP-guided partitioning and locally trained Recursive Feature Machines is well motivated: it supports heterogeneous feature relevance while bounding individual kernel-system sizes.
The evaluation is broad, covering 300 TALENT datasets, 51 TabArena-Lite datasets, and 17 larger meta-test datasets, with relevant GBDT, neural-network, and tabular foundation-model comparisons.

The reported TALENT regression results are strong: xRFM achieves average rank 4.70 and shifted geometric mean error 0.311, compared with 6.55 and 0.323 for TabPFN-v2. The larger regression datasets provide additional encouraging evidence.
The manuscript provides algorithmic pseudocode, hyperparameter search spaces, and illustrative examples showing how leaf-specific AGOPs expose different feature sensitivities.
weaknesses: The central contribution is insufficiently isolated experimentally. There are no reported controlled ablations separating AGOP-guided splitting, generalized kernels, diagonal AGOPs, and other leaf-RFM changes. Section 3.2 claims superiority over random/PCA splitting without presenting quantitative comparisons. With a 60,000-sample leaf threshold, smaller benchmark datasets do not exercise the proposed tree mechanism.

There is a substantial results-reporting error: Tables B.8 and B.10 contain identical numerical results despite being labeled regression and binary classification, respectively. Figure 3F also shows different binary-classification ratings from Table B.10. This prevents verification of the full TabArena binary results.

The runtime claims lack sufficient experimental controls. TALENT timing measures only the selected configuration, excluding the acknowledged approximately 100-fold tuning overhead, and hardware and execution settings are not adequately specified. This does not establish end-to-end computational superiority, particularly against TabPFN-v2. The TabArena total-training results are useful but do not resolve these broader comparison issues.

The claimed balanced-tree complexity requires qualifications absent from the algorithm. Thresholding at the median does not guarantee equal partitions when projections tie; Algorithm A.2 can recurse without reducing the dataset if all projections coincide. A tie-handling or stopping rule is needed, particularly for categorical and duplicated data. Scaling to 'essentially unlimited' data is also stronger than the experiments up to 500,000 samples support.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful pseudocode: numerical settings for split-model sample size and regularization, iteration limits, full tuning protocols, and conversion of kernel-regression outputs into probabilities for log-loss evaluation are insufficiently specified. Uncertainty estimates and paired comparisons against the strongest competing models are also missing; the reported Wilcoxon tests concern KRR and original RFM.

Interpretability evidence is primarily qualitative. AGOP measures squared gradient sensitivity and loses the overall sign of prediction changes; its eigenvectors alone do not justify directional conclusions such as benign cells having less uniform compactness. Feature-scaling sensitivity, stability across fits, and quantitative recovery or attribution comparisons are not evaluated.

The reported predictive performance is promising, but unresolved reporting inconsistencies and missing component-level evidence prevent establishing that the proposed local feature-learning mechanism delivers the claimed advantages. These are substantial gaps for a top-tier conference submission.

strengths: The method offers a coherent and practically useful combination of AGOP-guided partitioning and locally adapted kernel models. Learning different feature metrics in different leaves is a meaningful extension of global RFMs.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 300 TALENT datasets, 51 TabArena-Lite datasets, and 17 larger meta-test datasets. Regression results are particularly promising: Table B.1 reports an average rank of 4.70 versus 6.55 for TabPFN-v2, with top-three finishes on 56% of datasets.

The paper compares against strong tree, neural-network, and foundation-model baselines. Large-dataset results averaged over five splits and comparisons against kernel ridge regression and standard RFM provide additional positive evidence.
The appendix provides pseudocode and hyperparameter search spaces, and the synthetic example clearly illustrates the intended benefit of learning local feature structure.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not isolated experimentally. There are no quantitative ablations comparing AGOP splits with random, PCA, or axis-aligned splits, despite the assertion that AGOP splitting performs better. Comparisons with original RFM simultaneously change kernels, feature-matrix choices, tuning, and partitioning. With a 60,000-sample leaf threshold, smaller datasets do not exercise the proposed tree mechanism at all.

The efficiency claims need stronger experimental controls. TALENT timings cover only the selected hyperparameter configuration, excluding the substantial search overhead acknowledged in the text. Hardware, software settings, and timing comparability with imported benchmark results are insufficiently documented. Figure B.1 supplies useful scaling evidence on one dataset, but does not establish scalability to 'essentially unlimited' data.

The claimed balanced-tree guarantee is incomplete. Algorithm A.2 sends every projection equal to the median to the same child, so tied projections can produce unequal splits or even prevent recursive progress. This matters for categorical and repeated tabular inputs. The stated complexity requires a tie-handling or stopping rule and explicit assumptions that leaf size, dimension, and fitting budgets remain fixed.

Interpretability claims exceed what the analysis establishes. AGOP captures average gradient products, not signed prediction effects or causal relationships. Eigenvectors have arbitrary overall sign, and gradient outer products discard overall gradient sign. Consequently, the breast-cancer conclusion about benign versus malignant cells does not follow from the displayed eigenvector alone. Quantitative faithfulness, stability, and feature-recovery evaluations are absent.

Uncertainty and reproducibility reporting remain incomplete. The main benchmark comparisons lack confidence intervals or paired significance analyses against the strongest competitors; the reported Wilcoxon tests concern KRR and original RFM. Important implementation choices, including split-model sample size and parameters, iteration limits, and classification probability construction for log-loss evaluation, are not sufficiently specified.

The broad results support a promising regression method, but establish the proposed mechanism less convincingly than the headline claims suggest. Controlled component ablations and a reproducible, end-to-end compute comparison are needed to move this submission above the acceptance threshold.

strengths: xRFM offers a useful combination of supervised AGOP-based partitioning and locally adaptive kernel models, addressing both scalability and heterogeneous feature relevance.

The TALENT evaluation is substantial: 300 datasets and strong tree, neural-network, and foundation-model baselines. Regression results are particularly promising, with average rank 4.70 and shifted geometric mean error 0.311, versus 6.55 and 0.323 for TabPFN-v2.
Additional TabArena-Lite and large-dataset experiments broaden the evidence. Comparisons against standard RFM and kernel ridge regression show statistically significant improvements.
The manuscript provides algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter search spaces, and illustrative examples of local feature recovery.
weaknesses: The central architectural contribution is insufficiently isolated. There are no quantitative ablations separating supervised partitioning, generalized kernels, diagonal AGOP, and other modifications. The claimed superiority over random-projection and PCA splits is unsupported by reported comparisons, and leaf-size sensitivity is deferred to future work.

Runtime comparisons need stronger controls and documentation. TALENT timings exclude hyperparameter search, hardware and execution settings are unspecified, and tuning-budget parity is unclear. These omissions weaken the headline efficiency claims despite the encouraging measured runtimes.

The TabArena reporting contains a material error: Table B.10, labeled binary classification, duplicates the regression results in Table B.8 and does not match Figure 3F. Corrected results are needed to verify this portion of the evaluation.

Interpretability evidence is mostly qualitative. AGOP measures average gradient sensitivity; it does not establish causal effects or the direction of association with malignancy. The breast-cancer interpretation overreaches because an outer-product matrix loses the overall gradient sign. Stability and quantitative faithfulness are not evaluated.

The unconditional scalability claims require qualification. Median thresholding does not guarantee balanced, nonempty children when projections tie; Algorithm A.2 provides no fallback, potentially preventing termination on discrete or duplicated data. The stated complexity assumes balanced splits and fixed feature dimension and leaf size, while empirical scaling reaches only hundreds of thousands of samples.

Uncertainty is inadequately characterized for comparisons with leading baselines: the reported significance tests concern KRR and original RFM, while benchmark-level confidence intervals are absent. The broad positive results make the paper promising, but the missing ablations and reporting issues leave it slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Strong regression results across a substantial benchmark: on 100 TALENT datasets, xRFM achieves average rank 4.70 versus 6.55 for TabPFN-v2, and wins against CatBoost and XGBoost on 74% and 81% of datasets, respectively.

Evaluation extends beyond TALENT to TabArena-Lite and larger meta-test datasets, with the latter averaged over five splits. This provides meaningful evidence of practical utility across different evaluation protocols.

Combining local RFM feature learning with supervised tree partitioning is a coherent approach to scaling adaptive kernels. The synthetic example clearly illustrates its ability to recover different relevant features in different subpopulations.

The appendix supplies algorithms, hyperparameter ranges, detailed results, and comparisons of splitting strategies and soft routing. TabArena-Lite results support an attractive regression accuracy–inference-time tradeoff.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the main architectural contribution. Table E.3 identifies only seven TALENT datasets requiring splits, all classification tasks; therefore, the headline regression gains primarily demonstrate the modified leaf RFM. Comparisons against original RFM simultaneously change kernels, feature-matrix constraints, and other settings. Matched ablations of these components, partitioning, and leaf size are needed.

Runtime comparisons lack essential reproducibility details, including hardware and sufficiently explicit timing and tuning protocols. TALENT reports the best configuration's runtime while excluding hyperparameter search, which the paper acknowledges can introduce approximately 100-fold overhead. This limits conclusions about practical training efficiency, particularly against pretrained methods.

Scalability claims exceed the evidence. Experiments reach approximately 500,000 samples, with a controlled scaling curve on one dataset and no memory-scaling analysis. Fixed-size leaves explain asymptotic scaling in sample count, but substantial kernel-solver costs and dependence on feature dimension remain. Moreover, median-threshold splitting does not guarantee balanced partitions with tied projections; Algorithm A.2 provides no safeguard against an unchanged child and nontermination.

The interpretability discussion overstates what AGOP establishes. AGOP measures average gradient sensitivity and is unchanged when the predictor's sign is reversed; its eigenvectors cannot establish whether a feature increases malignancy. Off-diagonal gradient products also do not establish synergistic interactions. The biological interpretation and interaction claims require additional evidence, while explanation stability and faithfulness are not quantitatively evaluated.

Gradient computation is insufficiently specified for the proposed kernel family. The search permits p < 1, where derivatives can be singular when individual coordinate differences vanish, including between distinct samples with categorical features. Omitting self-kernel contributions, as described in Appendix A.4, does not resolve this issue. The numerical convention or smoothing mechanism should be stated and assessed.

The distinctive value of AGOP splitting remains uncertain: RF splitting with temperature tuning achieves better aggregate regression error and essentially matching classification error in Tables E.1–E.2. Missing matched comparisons against scalable kernel alternatives further weaken attribution of the reported gains. Overall, the predictive results are promising, but the ablation, reproducibility, and technical gaps leave the submission slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The predictive results are substantial, especially for regression. Across 100 TALENT regression datasets, xRFM achieves the best reported average rank (4.70) and shifted geometric mean error (0.311), outperforming strong GBDT and neural baselines.

Evaluation spans three benchmarks, including 300 TALENT datasets, 51 TabArena-Lite datasets, and 17 larger meta-test datasets. TabArena-Lite provides additional evidence of a useful accuracy–inference-cost tradeoff beyond the primary benchmark.

Combining locally trained feature-learning kernels with supervised tree partitioning is a coherent and practically useful approach. With bounded leaf sizes and balanced splits, the proposed structure offers favorable computational scaling.

The appendix supplies pseudocode, hyperparameter search spaces, detailed results, split-method comparisons, and five-split averages for the large-dataset evaluation. These are meaningful supporting materials.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the central contribution. Comparisons against original RFM simultaneously change the kernel family, diagonal/full AGOP selection, implementation, and partitioning. Most TALENT datasets do not require splitting at the 60,000-sample threshold, and Table E.3 identifies only seven that do. A controlled comparison against the improved leaf RFM without partitioning, together with component and leaf-size ablations, is needed to establish how much the proposed tree mechanism contributes.

The evidence for choosing AGOP splits over simpler supervised splits is limited. In Tables E.1–E.2, random-forest splitting with temperature tuning matches or improves the aggregate errors of AGOP splitting with temperature tuning. The results support supervised partitioning more clearly than they establish a distinctive advantage of the proposed AGOP rule.

The efficiency claims need stronger experimental controls and clearer qualification. TALENT timing measures only the selected configuration, excluding the tuning cost used to obtain its accuracy. Hardware, CPU/GPU allocation, and timing procedures are not adequately specified. Table E.11 also shows substantial total training costs for tuned xRFM. Thus, fast selected-model execution does not establish inexpensive end-to-end model selection.

Interpretability claims exceed what AGOP establishes. AGOP measures average gradient outer products and is unchanged when a scalar predictor is negated; its eigenvectors therefore cannot establish whether a feature increases or decreases malignancy. The breast-cancer conclusion about benign versus malignant cells is unsupported by the displayed eigenvector alone. Likewise, off-diagonal gradient correlations do not establish synergistic feature interactions. Quantitative faithfulness, stability, and comparative explanation evaluations are absent.

The scalability guarantee assumes balanced, progressing splits, but Algorithm A.2 does not handle tied median projections. With discrete or repeated feature values, the stated inequalities can produce highly unequal children or an unchanged child, invalidating the unconditional balance claim and potentially preventing termination. The claim of essentially unlimited scale also extends beyond experiments capped at roughly 500,000 samples; memory, feature-dimensionality costs, and broader scaling measurements are missing.

Experimental reproducibility and uncertainty remain incomplete despite the useful appendix. The manuscript does not fully specify benchmark-specific tuning budgets, split-model settings, iteration limits, or classification probability processing. Most headline comparisons lack uncertainty estimates, and the large-dataset comparisons omit stronger recent methods such as TabM despite citing them. These gaps limit confidence in the breadth of the superiority claims.

strengths: Strong empirical regression results: across 100 TALENT datasets, xRFM achieves an average rank of 4.70 versus 6.55 for TabPFN-v2, and shifted geometric mean error of 0.311 versus 0.323. Its reported win rates against CatBoost and XGBoost are 74% and 81%, respectively.

The combination of locally trained feature-learning kernels and supervised tree partitioning is practically motivated. Bounded leaf sizes offer a plausible route to scaling kernel methods while retaining local feature adaptation.

Evaluation covers three benchmarks, diverse strong baselines, and datasets reaching 500,000 samples. The appendix includes split-method comparisons, five-split meta-test results, and analyses of benchmark overlap.
The synthetic example clearly illustrates recovery of different relevant features in different subpopulations. Pseudocode and hyperparameter search spaces provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The experiments do not adequately isolate the central contribution. With a 60,000-sample leaf threshold, most TALENT datasets do not exercise tree partitioning; Table E.3 identifies only seven splitting datasets, all classification tasks. Comparisons against original RFM simultaneously change kernels, diagonal feature learning, and partitioning. A controlled comparison against the improved leaf RFM without splitting, component ablations, and leaf-size sensitivity are needed. Moreover, Tables E.1–E.2 do not establish an accuracy advantage for AGOP splitting over random-forest splitting.

Efficiency and reproducibility claims lack essential supporting detail. TALENT timing excludes hyperparameter search and measures only the selected configuration, despite substantial tuning overhead. Hardware, comparable resource allocation, exact tuning protocols across benchmarks, and several algorithm settings are insufficiently specified. This limits confidence in the strongest speed comparisons.

The balanced-tree complexity argument needs qualification. Algorithm A.2 sends every projection equal to the median to the same child; repeated or discrete projections can therefore produce unbalanced splits or even prevent recursion from making progress. No tie-handling or fallback is specified. The complexity also hides substantial dependence on leaf size and feature dimension, and experiments up to 500,000 samples do not establish practical scalability to 'essentially unlimited' data.

The interpretation claims exceed what AGOP establishes. Gradient outer products measure model sensitivity and are invariant to reversing the predictor's sign. Consequently, eigenvector signs alone cannot support the directional malignancy conclusion in Section 5. Real-data examples provide plausible narratives but no quantitative assessment of explanation fidelity, stability, or robustness to correlated features.

Performance claims require more careful reconciliation with the supplementary results. For example, Table E.13 places tuned xRFM below several competing tuned methods on both Elo and normalized score, making the stated top-three binary classification result unclear. Tables E.11–E.13 also show substantial dependence on tuning and ensembling. Consistent reporting of configurations, aggregation rules, and uncertainty is needed before drawing broad state-of-the-art conclusions.
